judge_assessment.explanation: Every system re-solves to the judge's values: (2,3), (3,2), (2,0), (1,3), no solution, (5,40), infinitely many, (2,2), (−1,2). I checked the two hardest cases directly against verify.py's own report in gate_log.txt: problem 5 returns PASS with 'inconsistent: no solution, as the key states' — the checker's dedicated branch for an empty expected — and problem 7 returns MANUAL with 'listed solution(s) valid but the system has a parametric/infinite family — verify completeness by hand'. That is exactly right, and the key's treatment of both is excellent. What the verdict misses is what happens to those two results when they reach the printed page. The Quick Answers bank reads '5. —' and '10. —'. Problem 10 is the genuine manual item; problem 5 is a VERIFIED no-solution whose expected list is empty, and render_entry returns '---' whenever the joined text is empty, so a proved answer and an unchecked one print the same glyph. This is the same failure mode as the canonical relation defect but via a different code path (the empty-list branch rather than the SympifyError branch), so it needs its own key and its own remedy. Second, the bank prints '7. x = 1, y = 4' — a single ordered pair — as the answer to a stem that asks 'How many ordered pairs make both equations true? Name two of them, then describe the whole solution set.' The answer is 'infinitely many; every point on y = −2x + 6', the key says so, and verify.py itself returned MANUAL for that id; the bank reflects none of it. Third, three problems print prose slots with no manual entry: 5's 'What the graph shows:', 6's 'What it means for a customer:' and 9's 'What went wrong:'. Problem 6 also asks 'Which shop is cheaper for 3 hours?' — 24 against 30 — which is machine-checkable and unchecked. The ACCEPT stands; the perfect answer_key_quality does not.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 5 and 7 are the two degenerate cases posed as ordinary graphing tasks rather than as vocabulary, and the key answers each twice — what the picture shows and what the algebra leaves behind (1 = −3 for the parallel pair, y = −2x + 6 twice for the coincident pair). That pairing of picture and leftover sentence is the thing to preserve.

Problem 9 gives a point, (2,−1), that lies on NEITHER line and asks the student to test it in both equations before correcting it. Testing a wrong point in both equations is the habit the directions demand ('a graph read by eye can be a square off'), and the item makes the student do it rather than read about it.

Problem 6's break-even is a real modelling item: y = 15 + 5x against y = 8x crossing at (5,40), with the key explaining that the crossing is where the cheaper shop CHANGES rather than a fact about 5 hours — and asking which shop is cheaper for 3 hours to force that reading.

Every problem's layout puts the grid on the left and the ordered pair plus the substitution check on the right, so the check is part of the answer rather than an afterthought; the study guide's first section spends its rule box on why substituting into BOTH equations is not optional.

root_causes.description: render_quick_answers.py::render_entry returns '---' in two unrelated situations: when a problem id has no expecteds at all (a manual item) and when the joined text of its expecteds is empty (a verified empty solution set). A proved 'no solution' and an unchecked open response therefore print the same glyph, in the same bank, three rows apart.
evidence: verify.json id 5: {"type": "solve", "expr": "2*x + 1 - (2*x - 3)", "expected": []}; gate_log.txt line 26 area records it PASS as an inconsistent system.
verify.json id 10 is the only {"type": "manual"} entry.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '5. —' and '10. —' — identical text for a PASSED check and a hand-graded item.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py lines 71-76: `vals = [...]; if not vals: return "---"` and `return text if text else "---"`.

root_causes.description: The bank prints `expected` regardless of what the verifier CONCLUDED about it. For a dependent system the expected point is a witness, not the answer, and verify.py explicitly downgrades that id to MANUAL — a status the bank has no way to represent, so the row asserts a definite single answer to a question whose answer is an infinite family.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 7 asks for the count of solutions, two examples, and the whole solution set.
gate_log.txt: '👁 [MANUAL] Problem 7: system[...] listed solution(s) valid but the system has a parametric/infinite family'.
answer_key.pdf bank row: '7. x = 1, y = 4'; the same key's worked solution boxes 'infinitely many solutions; e.g. (1, 4) and (2, 2)'.

root_causes.description: Problems that combine a verified point with printed prose slots record only the point. The classification sentence, the contextual interpretation and the error diagnosis are each a labelled response line on the worksheet with nothing behind them in the JSON, and problem 6's second numeric ask is unchecked as well.
evidence: Problem 5 prints three labelled slots — 'Slope of each line:', 'Number of solutions:', 'What the graph shows:' — against one solve entry.

Problem 6 prints 'What it means for a customer:' and 'Which shop is cheaper for 3 hours?' against one system entry; the comparison (3 hours: 30 dollars against 24) is machine-checkable and never checked.
Problem 9 prints 'What went wrong:' against one system entry; only problem 10 carries a manual entry.

improvements.title: Print a verified empty solution set as 'no solution', never as the manual em dash
improvements.proposed_change: In render_quick_answers.py::render_entry, distinguish 'the id has no expecteds' (manual) from 'the id has an expected that is an EMPTY collection' (a verified empty solution set). The second must render as 'no solution' or $\varnothing$, and the manual case should be marked as such (e.g. '— (manual)'), so the bank never uses one glyph for two verification states. This is a sibling of quick-answer-bank-drops-relation-answers and quick-answers-must-not-typeset-python-builtins — same module, different remedy — and whoever fixes one should fix all three.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture verify JSON with id 1 = {"type": "solve", "expected": []} and id 2 = {"type": "manual"}. Assert today's generator emits identical row text for both (it does — curr-261's shipped bank prints '5. —' and '10. —'); after the fix row 1 must read 'no solution' and row 2 must carry the manual marker.
improvements.expected_impact: On every parallel-lines, empty-set or no-real-solution item, the grader can see that the answer was proved rather than skipped. 'No solution' is itself a taught answer in this topic, so printing it as a dash removes the row that matters most.
improvements.risk: Low. Care is needed that an empty expected on a type where it means something else (a legitimately empty list of extraneous roots, say) still renders sensibly; the fixture should include one such case.

improvements.title: Bank the solution SET for a dependent system, not one witness point
improvements.proposed_change: When verify.py reports an id as MANUAL because the system is a parametric/infinite family, the bank must print that conclusion — 'infinitely many: y = −2x + 6 (e.g. (1,4), (2,2))' — rather than the witness point stored in `expected`. Concretely: propagate the per-id verification STATUS into the bank generator (it already reads the same JSON the verifier consumes), and use the answer_display field proposed for curr-257 to carry the set description. The witness point stays in `expected` so the validity check is unchanged.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture with a dependent two-equation system (2*x + y - 6, 4*x + 2*y - 12) whose expected is {x: 1, y: 4}. Assert the current bank row is exactly 'x = 1, y = 4' (curr-261's shipped key proves it) and that after the fix the row names infinitely many solutions and the line. The independent-system fixture must be unchanged.
improvements.expected_impact: Stops the grading strip from asserting a unique answer to a question whose taught answer is 'infinitely many', on precisely the item type where one-solution / none / infinitely many is the thing being assessed.
improvements.risk: Requires the generator to know the verifier's per-id status, which today it does not read; the simplest implementation re-runs the check, so build time grows slightly. Alternatively persist the status into the verify report the build already produces.

improvements.title: Declare the classification, interpretation and diagnosis slots in problems 5, 6 and 9
improvements.proposed_change: Add manual entries to ids 5, 6 and 9 carrying the acceptance criteria the key already states — for 5, 'same slope, different y-intercept' or 'they never meet' rather than just 'zero'; for 6, that the crossing is where the cheaper shop changes; for 9, that the student's point satisfies only one equation. The stem-scanning gate proposed across this batch would catch all three, since each prints a labelled prose slot ('What the graph shows:', 'What it means for a customer:', 'What went wrong:').
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet rendering a labelled prose slot ('What went wrong:') inside a \problem body whose verify id holds only a system entry. The gate must exit non-zero naming that id; adding a manual entry must make it pass.
improvements.expected_impact: The reported manual count (2 today) becomes the honest 5, and the key's existing grading notes get a formal home in the verification record instead of living only in prose.
improvements.risk: Low. Labelled prose slots are easy to detect because the template renders them as a bolded label followed by a rule, which is a different macro from \answerline.

improvements.title: Check problem 6's 'which shop is cheaper for 3 hours' comparison
improvements.proposed_change: Problem 6 prints a second numeric ask — at x = 3, Harbor costs 15 + 5·3 = 30 and Bayside 8·3 = 24, so Bayside is cheaper — and verify.json id 6 carries only the break-even system. Add a compare entry over the two evaluated costs so the sub-answer is proved and appears in the bank. Generally, a modelling item that asks the student to read the graph on ONE side of the crossing needs a check on that side, not only on the crossing itself.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: a break-even problem whose stem asks 'Which shop is cheaper for 3 hours?' with a verify id holding only the system entry. The coverage gate must fail naming the uncovered comparison; adding a compare entry must make it pass.
improvements.expected_impact: The interpretation half of a break-even item — which line is lower, and where — becomes verified rather than asserted, and the answer the student writes on the second line has a checked value behind it.
improvements.risk: Minimal; it adds one entry per modelling item. The compare entry must be authored over evaluated costs rather than symbols so the bank row stays readable.

case_summary: A complete, accurate and well-scaffolded graphical-systems set: ten problems covering read-the-crossing, graph-then-read, and the three classification cases, with every system re-solving correctly and the checker handling both degenerate cases properly — a PASS for the inconsistent pair and an honest MANUAL for the dependent one. The worked key is excellent, giving picture and algebra for each special case and a grading note where a written component exists. The defects are all downstream of the verification into the printed grading strip: problem 5's verified 'no solution' prints as the same em dash as problem 10's genuine manual item, and problem 7's infinite family prints as the single pair 'x = 1, y = 4' even though verify.py downgraded that id to MANUAL. Alongside that, three labelled prose slots (5, 6, 9) and one numeric sub-answer (6) have no entry. The mathematics deserves the 32/32; the answer key's quick bank does not.
